questions.q: You take home {t} a month. Using the 50/30/20 split, how much would go to saving each month?
questions.why: 20% of {t} = {answer}. 50% would go on needs and 30% on wants.

questions.q: You want {g} and can save {m} a month. Ignoring interest, how many months will it take? (Round up to whole months.)
questions.why: {g} ÷ {m} = {answer} months (rounded up). Interest shortens it slightly, but for small short goals the habit matters most.

questions.q: Sort each cost into need or want by matching it.
pairs: Bus pass to get to work
questions.why: Needs are what you must pay to live and work. Wants are choices, even if they're nice ones.

questions.q: What does AER tell you about a savings account?
options: What you'd earn in a year including compounding, so you can compare accounts fairly
The highest rate the bank has ever paid
How much tax you'll pay on the interest
questions.why: AER (Annual Equivalent Rate) includes the effect of interest being added during the year, so accounts paying monthly and yearly can be compared.

questions.q: A regular saver paying 7% on £200 a month earns about 7% of the £2,400 you pay in over the year.
questions.why: Money goes in month by month, so on average only about half of it is in the account. It earns about £90, roughly 3.75% of £2,400.

questions.q: Put these accounts in order from easiest to reach your money to hardest.
questions.why: Easy access is instant; notice accounts need warning; fixed bonds lock money away for the term.

questions.q: Where should an emergency fund usually be kept?
options: Mixed in with your spending money
questions.why: It must be reachable the same day and not fall in value. Keeping it separate stops it being spent by accident.

questions.q: Your essential costs are {e} a month. Using the lower end of MoneyHelper's guide (three months), how big should your emergency fund be?
questions.why: 3 × {e} = {answer}. The guide is three to six months of essential costs, which means needs only, not wants.

questions.q: Your bank fails. What protects your savings?
options: The FSCS pays back up to £120,000 per person per banking licence
The bank's insurance pays back everything, however much
The government pays back any amount
questions.why: The Financial Services Compensation Scheme covers up to £120,000 per person per banking licence (from 1 December 2025).

questions.q: Explain why "saving whatever's left at the end of the month" often doesn't work, and what works better.

ideas.label: Spending grows to use up what's there, so there's rarely anything left
Save first: move a set amount on payday (automatically), then spend the rest
any: as soon as you get paid

questions.model: Spending tends to grow to fill whatever's in the account, so by the end of the month there's rarely anything left. It works better to pay yourself first: move a set amount to savings automatically on payday and live on the rest.

tests.answer: You usually spend it all so nothing is left. Set up a standing order to save on payday instead.
Because you end up spending everything you have.

questions.topic: rates matter more as the pot grows
questions.q: Saving £150 a month for 10 months, a 4.5% account earns only about £19 more than a 1% account. Explain why, and when the rate starts to matter more.

ideas.label: The pot is small and builds up gradually over a short time, so little interest is earned either way
The rate matters more with a bigger balance or over a longer time

questions.model: The pot is small and only builds up month by month over a short time, so little interest is earned in either account. The rate matters much more with a bigger balance or over a longer time: £5,000 for a year earns about £175 more at 4.5% than at 1%.
questions.why: For small, short goals the habit matters most; for bigger pots the rate matters too.

tests.answer: The amount is small and it's only for a few months. With a bigger balance over years the rate makes a big difference.
Because it is a small amount of money.
Because banks don't pay interest monthly.
